tagline: A winding valley road links river crossings and former wagon trails.
intro: The Sheyenne River Valley Scenic Byway follows a winding road through a valley dotted with trees, towns and farmsteads. The Federal Highway Administration presents this National Scenic Byway as a change from North Dakota’s flat horizons, with bridges, trails and historic sites along its 63 miles. Its suggested nine hours allows for experiencing the whole byway. The valley was cut by torrents of glacial meltwater about 13,000 years ago, leaving a trench that reaches 330 feet deep and a mile wide.

Part of the road follows an older path: the valley route from Highway 46 to Fort Ransom began as an Indigenous footpath. The Valley City tourism bureau credits settler Amos Olson with clearing most of the road between Preston and Fort Ransom. North Dakota designated the byway in 1997; a 16-mile extension in 2000 brought in the Baldhill Dam area, and national designation followed in 2002.

At the northern end, Baldhill Dam was completed in 1951 after a local water-conservation association urged its construction for water storage and flood control. Begin at Getchell Township Hall on Highway 21 and follow the corridor past Baldhill Dam and the fish hatchery to Valley City’s bridge sites. Continue through Kathryn and Fort Ransom to finish at Lisbon.

moments.title: Hi-Line Railroad Bridge
moments.text: The Northern Pacific built the Hi-Line Railroad Bridge to avoid the steep grades into and out of the Sheyenne valley. Its old route descended to a low bridge in Valley City before climbing out again; the new crossing moved one mile upstream. Regular service began in 1908. The bridge stretches 3,860 feet, stands 162 feet above the river and carries BNSF freight trains. Its 61 spans rest on 30 steel towers, giving the crossing its long succession of supports. Two of its longer spans cross the Sheyenne; a third passes over the former Soo Line tracks.
moments.notice: Look for the steel towers supporting the bridge’s 61 spans.

moments.title: Fort Ransom
moments.text: Cut stones from the abandoned fort became part of the foundation of T. J. Walker’s general store. Built in 1907–08, that store has housed the Ransom County Historical Society’s museum since 1972. The fort itself was established in 1867 to protect wagon trains, settlers and railroad workers. When the railroad went farther north, Fort Seward was built at Jamestown and Fort Ransom was abandoned in 1872. The store also held the Fort Ransom post office in the 1960s; it joined the mill, dam and former ice house in a historic district in 1979.

moments.title: Lisbon
moments.text: Lisbon’s name came from New York: founder Joseph L. Colton named the town for his wife’s hometown when he established it in 1880. Downtown, the Scenic movie theater dates to 1911. During the 2020 pandemic, it kept showing films by moving screenings outdoors.
